explanations.explanation: That's the word. David says, 'I shall not want,' which is the old-school way of saying he'll never lack what he needs. The shepherd's already got it handled. Friend, when the LORD's your shepherd, you're not out here making grocery lists.
David doesn't say that. He says 'I shall not want,' meaning he won't lack anything. The shepherd provides; the sheep doesn't clock in for it. Different arrangement entirely.
That's not what David says. 'I shall not want' means he won't be without what he needs, not that he won't misplace it. The shepherd's keeping track, friend.

That's the one. Green grass to lie down in, quiet water to drink. David's not painting a hustle culture poster here. The shepherd's not driving the sheep; he's settling them down. That's the whole mood.
Nah, David's lying down. The grass is green, the water's quiet. There's no grind in this picture. The LORD's not a boss with a clipboard; he's a shepherd making sure the sheep can breathe.
Not here. That comes later in the valley. This verse is all about the safe place, the green pasture, the still water. David's showing what the shepherd provides before the hard road hits.
That's it. 'He restores my soul.' The LORD doesn't just feed David and water him; he goes deeper and brings his soul back to where it needs to be. Full service, inside and out.
David doesn't say that here. The LORD restores his soul, brings it back to health. Testing's not in this line. This is about care, not examination.
Nope. David says 'restores,' not 'weighs.' The shepherd's not out here measuring souls on a scale. He's bringing David's soul back to where it belongs.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: That's what David says. 'For the sake of His name.' The LORD guides him in righteousness because it honors who the LORD is. The shepherd's reputation is on the line, and he comes through.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say that. It's 'for the sake of His name.' The reason is about the LORD's own character and glory, not about the flock as a group. Close, but not the text.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: That's not in there. David says 'for the sake of His name.' The land's not mentioned. It's about who the LORD is, not about territory.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: That's it. 'For You are with me.' That's the whole reason. The valley's still dark, the shadow's still there, but the shepherd's walking through it too. That's the difference.

David doesn't say that. He says 'I will fear no evil, for You are with me.' The courage comes from the shepherd's presence, not from David pulling himself up by his bootstraps. Sheep don't have boots anyway.
Nope. David never says how long the valley is. Could be a quick walk, could be miles. The point isn't the valley's length; it's who's in it with him.

That's right. David says it plain: 'Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.' In a dark valley, those tools of the shepherd's trade aren't threats. They're proof he's watching, guiding, protecting. That's comfort.

Actually, David does say that. 'Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.' The rod and staff were tools a shepherd used to guide and guard the sheep. In the valley, they mean the shepherd's still on the job.
That's the word. 'You prepare a table before me.' David's not a sheep anymore in this picture; he's a guest, and the LORD's the host setting out a full spread. Upgrade of the century.
David doesn't say that. It's a table, not a tent. The picture's about being fed and honored as a guest, not about getting shelter. Different verse, different image.
Nope. It's a table. David's sitting down to eat, not lying down to sleep. The LORD's hosting a meal, not turning down the covers.
Actually, that's not what David says. He says 'in the presence of my enemies.' The table's right there where they can see it. The LORD's not hiding David away; he's honoring him out in the open.
Right. David says 'in the presence of my enemies,' not far away from them. The LORD prepares this table where the enemies can watch David eat. That's bold hospitality, friend.
That's the picture. 'My cup overflows.' Not full, not nicely topped off. Overflowing. Running over. The host keeps pouring past the brim. That's the kind of abundance David's talking about.
Nah, that's not it. The overflowing cup is the host's doing, not David's clumsiness. The LORD's the one pouring. This is abundance, not accident.
Nope. Nothing hurried here. An overflowing cup means the host is generous, not that David's trying to leave. This is a slow, honored meal, not a drive-through.

That's it. 'Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life.' Not maybe, not hopefully. Surely. Two things tracking David down every single day: goodness and mercy. That's a pursuit you want.
David doesn't say that. It's goodness and mercy. Those are the shepherd's gifts, not the world's rewards. Wealth and honor might show up, might not. Goodness and mercy are guaranteed.
Not what David says. Goodness and mercy are the pair. Strength and wisdom are great, but they're not in this line. David's looking at what the shepherd keeps sending his way, day after day.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. 'I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.' David's not talking real estate; he's talking home. The shepherd's house, the host's house, the place where he belongs for good.
David doesn't say that. Hebron was a real place, but it's not in this verse. The house of the LORD is where David's headed, and he's not putting a time limit on it. Forever.
Nope. Canaan's the promised land, but David's aiming higher than geography. 'The house of the LORD forever.' That's the destination, and it's not on any map the GPS knows.
